Wind turbines provided almost 8.4% of the total electricity generation in the United States in 2020.
There are more than 700,800 wind turbines running across 44 states in the US.
The four main types of wind turbine blade defects studied are: blade cracks, leading edge erosion, delamination, and lightning strike damage.
The virtual wind turbine models were designed using CAD software like SolidWorks and then modified to simulate 40 different defect scenarios.
A total of 642 synthetic images with corresponding semantic segmentation ground truth were generated using the Unity game engine and Perception Package.
The U-Net convolutional network architecture was used for image segmentation, trained for 100 epochs using the Adam optimizer and Dice Loss function.
The final Dice Coefficient on the test set was 0.658, indicating moderate segmentation accuracy.
The paper notes that using synthetic data helped overcome challenges like lack of real-world data, background biases, and inaccessibility of remote wind turbine locations.
Future work includes improving the segmentation model, adding a classification module, and evaluating on a wider range of defects and real wind turbine images.
Automated and accurate defect detection is crucial for wind turbine operations to avoid catastrophic failures and ensure uninterrupted power generation.
Traditional manual inspection of wind turbine blades is time-consuming and expensive, motivating the need for an automated solution.
The two-step approach of generating synthetic data and training a deep learning model addresses the challenge of limited real-world data.
Key advantages of the virtual reality and synthetic data approach include simulating diverse defect scenarios, controlling for background biases, and enabling remote and autonomous inspection.
The paper used the Jaccard Index and Dice Coefficient as evaluation metrics for the segmentation performance of the U-Net model.
The proposed methodology provides reasonable defect detection accuracy, making it suitable for autonomous and remote inspection through aerial vehicles like drones.
